questions.problem:
Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

A triangle $S$ has vertices at $(1,0)$, $(0,-3)$ and $(-2,1).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of ${S}^{′},$ the image of $S$ under the action of $T?$

- $(12,-24)$
- $(8,16)$
- $(2,-4)$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the image of $S$ under the action of $T$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S:$

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under $T$ by calculating the matrix product $TX:$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & -3 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 12 & -8 \\ -4 & -24 & 16\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of ${S}^{′}$ are $(2,-4)$, $(12,-24)$ and $(-8,16).$ 

So, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040372/assets/cfcbd4b374456b4a5913289592d875a42caf81fd02984180e68e34c5b82ef905.png)

Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

What would be the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any linear transformation $T$ with associated $2\times 2$ matrix $T,$ we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., $det(T)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., $det(T)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $T$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $T$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is the point $(0,0),$ the origin of the coordinate system.

Since $T$ is the zero matrix, the image of our object under the action of $T$ is the origin.

choices.value: The origin $O$ of the coordinate system
A point, different from the origin

answer_fields.correct_value: The origin $O$ of the coordinate system

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040372/assets/8978d3bb02b4032b6e3a8b4a85878db647eb8323ac5b0423b5a9a6fab121c7e7.png)

Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -2 & -8\end{aligned}].
$$

What would be the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any linear transformation $T$ with associated $2\times 2$ matrix $T,$ we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., $det(T)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., $det(T)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $T$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $T$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is the point $(0,0),$ the origin of the coordinate system.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Computing the determinant of $T,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -2 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot (-8)-4\cdot (-2) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. Therefore, the image of the triangle under the action of $T$ is a line segment.

choices.value: A point, different from the origin
The origin $O$ of the coordinate system

Consider the linear transformation $\mathbf T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

A triangle $S$ has vertices at $(-1,2), (0,1)$ and $(1,1).$ Which of the following are coordinates of the vertices of $S',$ the image of $S$ under the action of $\mathbf T?$

- $(-2,0)$

- $(0,0)$

- $(2,0)$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the image of $S$ under the action of $\mathbf T$, we first create a matrix $X$ containing all of the vertices of $S\mathbin{:}$

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we compute the image of $X$ under $\mathbf T$ by calculating the matrix product $TX\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}TX & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of the respective vertices of $S'$ are $(-2,0),$ $(0,0),$ and $(2,0).$

So, the correct answer is "I, II,  and III."

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14040372/assets/89efcd0ecb51dac08a1102c5a347eea3459f7209de7cbac0a88b192259ca3b7e.png)

Consider the linear transformation $\mathbf T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

What would be the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $\mathbf{T}?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with associated $2 \times 2$ matrix $T,$ we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is non-singular, i.e., $\det(T) \neq 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $\mathbf{T}$ is singular, i.e., $\det(T) = 0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $T$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $T$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is the point $(0,0),$ the origin of the coordinate system.

Since $T$ is the zero matrix, the image of our object under the action of $\mathbf{T}$ is the origin.
